content: Environmental impact assessment evaluates how human activities affect ecosystems across product and service lifecycles, providing frameworks for more sustainable decision-making. Life cycle assessment (LCA) systematically analyzes environmental impacts across a product's entire existenceâfrom raw material extraction through manufacturing, distribution, use, and disposal/recycling. Key environmental impact categories include climate change (measuring greenhouse gas emissions in carbon dioxide equivalentsâCOâe); resource depletion (quantifying consumption of finite materials and energy sources); water use (measuring volume consumed and pollution caused); land use change (assessing habitat conversion and biodiversity impacts); and pollution (evaluating emissions to air, water, and soil). Production phases often create significant environmental burdens: extractive processes like mining consume energy, disturb landscapes, and potentially release toxins; manufacturing transforms raw materials into products using energy-intensive processes with various emissions; and agriculture contributes impacts through land conversion, fertilizer and pesticide application, and livestock methane emissions. Transportation between production stages adds impacts through fuel consumption and infrastructure requirementsâwith air freight typically generating higher emissions per ton-kilometer than sea or rail shipping. Consumer use phase contributions vary dramatically by product type: for appliances and vehicles, operational energy often dominates lifecycle impacts, while for items like clothing, production impacts may exceed use phase effects. Disposal creates environmental burdens through landfilling (generating methane and potential leachate), incineration (producing air emissions), or recycling (which saves resources but requires energy and processing). Environmental impacts extend beyond producers and consumers to affect communities near production facilities, wildlife in affected ecosystems, and future generations inheriting environmental degradationâthese externalized costs often remain absent from product pricing, creating market failures that policy interventions attempt to correct through regulations, taxes, or incentives.

scenario.title: Supply Chain Explorer
scenario.content: Students make shopping decisions and trace the environmental consequences through interactive supply chains, discovering how everyday choices connect to global impacts. The simulation allows students to select products across categories like food, clothing, electronics, and transportation, then visualizes the complex production networks behind these items. The system reveals normally hidden environmental effects including resource extraction, manufacturing processes, transportation routes, usage impacts, and end-of-life scenarios. Students can compare alternative products with different sourcing, production methods, and distribution systems, observing how these choices affect various environmental indicators. Interactive tools demonstrate concepts like carbon footprints, virtual water, land use change, and pollution burdens across product lifecycles. Challenge scenarios ask students to balance environmental considerations with other factors like price, performance, and social impacts, teaching nuanced sustainability thinking beyond simplistic good versus bad" categorizations."

hypothesis.description: Students will trace environmental consequences by analyzing product lifecycles and supply chains. They will identify how consumer choices connect to ecological effects across global systems, and evaluate alternatives based on multiple sustainability indicators and impact categories.
